objectives: Say what the people believed about the stone objects and what Abraham saw.
Support one simple idea with a sentence from the chapter.
Discover what “looked like” tells us, use common irregular past forms (grew, made, thought, saw, came), and notice the difference between “did not” (a fact) and “could not” (not able).
Describe an everyday object with “looks like” and “can / cannot”.
content.pedagogy: Start with meaning: Learners listen, then find what the people believed and what Abraham saw, each with a sentence from the text. The grammar grows out of the story sentence: You ask “Were the objects real people?” and learners discover that “looked like” is about shape, not about what a thing is. Then they compare “did not eat” with “could not move” and say which one means “not able” before you confirm it.
priorKnowledge: Simple action verbs (eat, drink, talk, move, hear) and “can / can’t” in the present.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners may read “looked like people” as “were people” or confuse “like” (similar) with “like” (love).
“did not” and “could not” are used as if they meant the same thing.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: looked like + noun (shape, not identity) · irregular past forms: grow → grew, make → made, think → thought, see → saw, come → came · did not / could not + base verb (a fact vs not able).
Notice (Activity 1): Board “These objects looked like people or animals.” Ask only: “Were they real people? What were they made of?” Learners answer from the text (stone) and say in their own words what “looked like” means before you confirm it.
Build (Activities 2–3): Match the base and past forms, then choose the base verb after “did not” and “could not” (did not worship, did not eat, could not move). Ask after each item: “Is this a fact, or is it about ability?”
Likely errors: *did not ate · *could not moved · *thinked / *seed · “looked like” read as “liked”.
Use (Activity 4): three or four sentences contrasting belief and observation (People believed … Abraham saw that … They could not …), then one sentence about a real object in the classroom (It looks like …, but it cannot …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the long sentence: “They could not MOVE | from one place to aNOTHer, | and they could not HEAR | or underSTAND their WISHes!”
-ed endings: named /d/, bowed /d/, believed /d/, loved /d/, looked /t/, talked /t/.
“could not” is often /kʊdnt/: model it once slowly, once at normal speed.
Word focus: MES-sen-ger, mes-o-po-TA-mi-a, BAB-y-lon, in-TEL-li-gent, HON-est (silent h).
beforeReading: Put a small stone and a toy animal on your desk. Ask: “What can this stone do? What can’t it do?” Collect three “It can’t …” ideas on the board as predictions for the chapter.
duringReading: First listening, books closed: Which of our “It can’t …” ideas are in the chapter?
Two columns: “People believed …” / “Abraham saw …”, one sentence from the text in each.
Underline every “did not” and “could not”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (why talking to the stone gods was silly).
Language Focus: Look at “looked like” (Activity 1), practise past forms and did not / could not (Activities 2–3), then use them (Activity 4).
Say one sentence about a classroom object with “It looks like …, but it cannot …”.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Hook: Stone and toy animal on the desk, learners say what the stone cannot do, three ideas stay on the board; 4–11 Listen with books closed (which ideas are in the chapter?), then listen and read along; 11–17 T-chart in pairs: “People believed …” / “Abraham saw …”, each with a sentence from the text, quick whole-class check; 17–21 Quick Challenge individually; 21–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Were they real people?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, learners read their answers aloud; 30–37 Use: Activity 4 orally in pairs, then each learner writes one “It looks like …, but it cannot …” sentence about a classroom object and two volunteers read it; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did the people believe about the stone objects?
What did Abraham see with his own eyes?
Which sentence shows a fact, and which shows that the objects were not able to do something?
interactiveTips: Use the Babylon hotspot for the place and the Stone Gods hotspot for the people’s belief.
Replay the last sentence of the chapter and ask learners to count the things the objects could not do.
Keep the lesson on what the text says; do not ask learners to judge people of other beliefs today.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give three frames: “People believed ____. The objects did not ____. They could not ____.” Learners copy the verbs from the text first.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences: One with “looked like”, one with “did not”, one with “could not” and one about a real object with “looks like … but cannot …”.

formativeAssessment: Gives one belief sentence and one observation sentence from the text.
Uses the base verb after “did not” and “could not”.
Explains “looked like” as shape, not identity.
expectedResponses: People believed the stone objects were their gods, but Abraham saw that they did not eat, drink or talk and could not move, hear or understand.
content.transferTask: Describe one object at home or in the classroom with “It looks like …” and “It can / cannot …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners find the meaning of “looked like” and the difference between “did not” and “could not” themselves before I confirmed it?

classroomManagement.instructions: Work with your partner. Make a T-chart: “People believed …” and “Abraham saw …”. Copy one sentence from the story under each.
checkQuestions: How many sentences do you copy? (two)
Where do they come from? (the story)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “did not eat, drink or talk” goes under “Abraham saw”. In the Use task, listen for the base verb after “cannot”. Choose two clear “It looks like …, but it cannot …” sentences to read aloud.

rubric: Past forms and base verb after did not / could not
exitTicket: Complete: “The objects looked like ____, but they could not ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Gives one belief sentence and one observation sentence from the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Read two sentences and ask “Is this what people believed or what Abraham saw?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Points to the sentence that proves the answer.
rubricLevels.notYet: Show the paragraph and ask the learner to underline the sentence.

rubricLevels.criterion: Past forms and base verb after did not / could not
rubricLevels.secure: Uses the base verb after did not and could not.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write “did not eat / did not ate” and ask which is right.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes one “It looks like …, but it cannot …” sentence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Hold up a classroom object and give the frame.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham lives among people who make stone objects and believe in them. The chapter shows what Abraham sees with his own eyes.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: The same person is İbrahim in Turkish, Ibrahim in Arabic and Abraham in English. Which other names in the book change in English (Hacer / Hagar, İsmail / Ishmael)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners notice that people in this story believed differently from Abraham. The chapter describes, it does not mock, so learners describe without laughing at anyone.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners say three sentences about Abraham and his town. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each tells the partner two facts without looking. The partner writes one of them.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 2 aloud. Asker asks “What could the stone objects not do?”. Writer lists the answers. Change roles for paragraph 1.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “What is a smart question a child can ask?” The learner gives one example and links it to Abraham.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Abraham was an honest and intelligent boy.” into their home language. Which words did each pair choose for “honest” and “intelligent”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what people in Abraham’s town did. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Paragraph 2 ends with an exclamation mark. Why does the writer use it here?” (It shows how surprising the wishes were.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Notes are short words in the right box. The retell gives at least two things the stone objects could not do.

objectives: Describe the father’s work and what he said about the idols.
Explain with the text why Abraham laughed at the explanation about Mardukh.
Discover the difference between habits (again and again) and one event (One day), and use used to + verb, bigger than, because and tell + person + not to + verb.
Talk about one childhood habit and one special day.
content.pedagogy: Use a simple gesture system: Arms in a circle for “again and again”, one finger for “one time”. Learners show the gesture while you read parts of the chapter, then sort the text parts in Activity 1. They discover that “sometimes” and “used to” tell us about habits and that “One day” opens one special event. Only after that do you name the rule.
priorKnowledge: Short adjectives (big, small), simple past verbs and “because”.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners think Abraham laughed only because the ears were big; the text shows he laughed at the father’s explanation (“He has big ears because he is very smart”).
“used to” is followed by -ing (*used to watching).
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: again and again (played, rode, sometimes kicked) vs one time (One day + past) · used to + base verb · bigger than · because + reason · tell + person + not to + verb.
Notice (Activity 1): Read “He rode on their backs and sometimes kicked them” and “One day, his father saw Abraham.” Ask: “Did this happen one time or many times? Which word tells you?” Learners find “sometimes” and “One day” and say the rule in their own words.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose “used to watch”, “bigger” and “because”, then build “He got angry and told his son not to play with it again.” Ask: “Where does ‘not’ go?”
Likely errors: *used to watching · *more big than · *told his son to not play / *told his son don’t play · “so” instead of “because”.
Use (Activity 4): a short exchange with a question, a comparison and a reason, then two sentences about the learners’ own childhood (When I was small, I used to … One day, …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Weak forms: “used to” /juːstə/, “than” /ðən/, “to” /tə/: “He TOLD his SON | not to PLAY with it aGAIN.”
Question intonation: “WHY do you MAKE and PUT these TOYS in the HOUSE?↘” (Wh- question falls).
Contrastive stress: “Its EARS are BIGger than OURS.”
Word focus: ri-DIC-u-lous, re-SPECT, PRES-ents (noun), I-dol, MAR-dukh.
beforeReading: Show the gestures (circle = again and again, one finger = one time). Say three sentences about yourself (“I drink tea every morning.” / “Last Monday I lost my key.”) and learners show the right gesture.
duringReading: Listen and show the gesture at “used to”, “sometimes” and “One day”.
Underline the father’s explanation about Mardukh’s ears.
Circle what made Abraham laugh.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (why Abraham found the explanation ridiculous).
Language Focus: Sort again and again / one time (Activity 1), practise used to, bigger than, because and told … not to (Activities 2–3), then ask, compare and explain (Activity 4).
Say one “I used to …” sentence and one “One day, …” sentence about your childhood.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Gesture warm-up with three sentences about the teacher; 4–11 Listen and show the gesture at “used to”, “sometimes” and “One day”, then read along; 11–17 Pairs underline the father’s explanation and answer: What did the father say? Why did Abraham laugh?; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs with gestures, Activity 2 individually, Activity 3 as a whole-class build on the board (Where does “not” go?); 30–37 Use: Pairs tell each other one “I used to …” and one “One day …” sentence about their childhood, then write them, and three learners read theirs; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Abraham do again and again with the idols?
What happened on one special day?
Why did the father’s explanation make Abraham laugh?
interactiveTips: Use the Idol Making hotspot for the father’s work and the Mardukh hotspot for the explanation about the ears.
Replay the father’s answer (“He has big ears because …”) before the Quick Challenge.
The dialogue is read by you or the audio; learners do not act out Abraham or his father.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give frames: “Abraham used to ____. One day, ____. The father said ____ because ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four connected sentences with used to, One day, bigger than and told … not to ….

formativeAssessment: Sorts habits and one-time events correctly and names the signal word.
Uses “used to + base verb” and “told … not to + verb”.
Gives the father’s explanation as the reason for Abraham’s laughter.
expectedResponses: The father made idols from stone and said Mardukh had big ears because he was very smart; Abraham found this explanation ridiculous and laughed.
content.transferTask: Tell a partner one thing you used to do as a small child and one special thing that happened one day.
content.teacherReflection: Did the gestures help learners hear the difference between a habit and one event before I named it?

classroomManagement.instructions: Listen and show the gesture when you hear “used to”, “sometimes” and “One day”. Then underline the father’s explanation with your partner.
checkQuestions: When do you show the gesture? (at used to, sometimes and One day)
What do you underline? (the father’s explanation)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Watch the gestures to see who confuses habit and one event. During the pair questions, check that learners give the big-ears explanation as the reason Abraham laughed. Listen in the Use task for “I used to + base verb”.

rubric: used to / bigger than / told … not to
exitTicket: Write one “When I was small, I used to …” sentence and one “My mother told me not to …” sentence.

rubricLevels.secure: Sorts habits and one-time events and names the signal word.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the three signal words on cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives the father’s explanation as the reason for the laugh.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What did the father say about Mardukh?”.

rubricLevels.criterion: used to / bigger than / told … not to
rubricLevels.secure: Uses used to + base verb, bigger than and told … not to.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes one “I used to …” and one “One day …” sentence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Tell your own example first as a model.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham's father makes and sells idols. Many cultures have family jobs that pass from parent to child.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which jobs pass from father or mother to child in Türkiye (a family shop, a carpet weaver, a farmer)? Are family businesses common in English-speaking countries too ('Smith & Sons')?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Children can respect their parents and still think differently. Learners say one polite English sentence for disagreeing with an older person.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note what Abraham’s father did and what Abraham asked.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners act the dialogue between Abraham and his father in four lines.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner why the father said Mardukh had big ears. The partner says why Abraham laughed.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Finder finds the father’s answer about the gods. Reader reads it aloud. Explainer says it in his or her own words.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “How do you ask your parents a hard question politely?” The learner gives one example.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Abraham’s father made idols.” into their home language. How does their home language say “idols”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham asked his father about the idols. Next lesson ask what their listener said.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Abraham calls the idols ‘toys’. Why does the writer use this word?” (It shows that the idols were only objects.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The dialogue keeps the facts of the chapter. The notes name Mardukh.

content.chapter: Chapter 3 — Abraham Looks at the Sky
objectives: Follow the same pattern for the star and the moon: question → what happened → conclusion.
Explain what happened to both the star and the moon.
Discover that “Could this be …?” asks if something is possible, understand the thinking words (always thought about, wanted to know, was in search of), and use Then, because and could not be.
Think through a new everyday mystery with a question, an observation and a conclusion.
content.pedagogy: Draw two columns on the board, Star and Moon, and three rows: question / what happened / conclusion. Learners fill the grid from the text and see that the pattern repeats. The grammar starts from the question: You ask “Is Abraham sure?” and learners discover that “Could this be …?” shows a possibility he is testing, not a belief.
priorKnowledge: Night and sky words (star, moon, dark) and simple past verbs.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners think Abraham believed the star was his Lord; the question shows he was testing an idea.
The star and the moon are treated as two different stories instead of one repeated pattern.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: Could this be …? (asking if something is possible) · thinking words: always thought about, wanted to know, was in search of · Then (next step) · because (reason) · could not be (conclusion: not possible).
Notice (Activity 1): Board “He saw a bright star and thought, ‘Could this be my Lord?’” Ask: “Is Abraham sure? What does he do next?” Learners say that he is asking himself and waiting to see.
Build (Activities 2–3): Match the thinking words with their meanings, then complete the night scene with Then / because / could not.
Likely errors: *Could this is …? · *wanted know · *in search for · *it could not was his Lord.
Use (Activity 4): three or four sentences about a new everyday mystery (a sound at night, a light in the street): Could this be …? When …, … It could / could not be … because ….
content.pronunciationFocus:
Yes/no question rises: “COULD this be my LORD?↗”
Pause before the reason: “I will not show reSPECT to it, | because it SETS | and disapPEARS.”
Contrastive stress: “alLAH NEVer goes aWAY!”
-ed endings: passed /t/, disappeared /d/, wanted /ɪd/, created /ɪd/.
Word focus: cre-A-tor, COUN-try-side, dis-ap-PEARED, SEARCH (one syllable).
beforeReading: Ask: “What changes in the night sky from evening to morning?” Pairs name two changes; keep them as predictions.
duringReading: Listen for gist: What did Abraham look at?
Fill the Star / Moon grid: question, what happened, conclusion.
Underline the three sentences about Abraham’s thinking in the first paragraph.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (put the events of the night in order).
Language Focus: Look at “Could this be …?” (Activity 1), practise thinking words and Then / because / could not (Activities 2–3), then use them (Activity 4).
Write one question-observation-conclusion chain about an everyday mystery.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Sky warm-up: Pairs name two changes in the night sky; 4–11 Listen for gist, then read along; 11–18 Star / Moon grid on the board, pairs fill one row each and read their sentence from the text aloud; 18–22 Quick Challenge: Learners order the events alone, then check with the Star / Moon grid; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Is Abraham sure?), Activities 2–3 in pairs; 31–37 Use: “Mystery sound” game, you make a sound behind your desk, pairs write “Could this be …? It could not be … because …” and read their guesses; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What happened to the star and to the moon?
Why do the questions not mean that Abraham believed in the star or the moon?
Which words show that Abraham was always thinking and searching?
interactiveTips: Use The Star and The Moon hotspots as the two columns of the grid.
Before the Quick Challenge, ask learners to say the order of the night aloud: cave, star, moon.
Replay “Could this be my Lord?” and ask learners whether the voice sounds sure or unsure.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Use the grid with the first words given: “Could this be ____? When it ____, he said ____. It could not be ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences connecting the star and the moon with Then, because and could not be.

formativeAssessment: Names the same change for the star and the moon.
Explains “Could this be …?” as a question about possibility.
Uses Then / because / could not be in a short chain.
expectedResponses: The star disappeared and the moon went away, so Abraham understood that they could not be his Lord because Allah never goes away.
content.transferTask: Think through a small everyday mystery with “Could this be …?”, one observation and one conclusion.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the repeated pattern themselves, and did they explain the question as testing an idea, not believing it?

classroomManagement.instructions: Look at the Star and Moon grid on the board. Each pair fills one row and reads their sentence from the story aloud.
checkQuestions: How many rows does your pair fill? (one)
Do you write your own sentence? (no, a sentence from the story)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that both rows show the same change: it went away. In the Mystery sound game, listen for “Could this be …?” with rising intonation. Note one good “It could not be … because …” sentence for the class.

exitTicket: Complete: “Could this be ____? No, it could not be ____ because ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Names the same change for the star and the moon.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What happened to the star? And to the moon?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Says “Could this be …?” is a question about possibility.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Is Abraham sure here?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses Then, because and could not be in a short chain.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the chain frame with three gaps.

rubricLevels.secure: Makes a new mystery chain in the game.
rubricLevels.notYet: Let the learner choose from two guesses on the board.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham watches the star, the moon and the sun. People in every culture have looked at the sky and asked questions.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Which Turkish words come from sky watching (Ülker for the Pleiades, Çoban Yıldızı for Venus)? What is the English name for each?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Different cultures named the stars differently. Learners enjoy the names without treating any old belief as foolish.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note what Abraham saw in the sky and what he said.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners tell the night in three sentences with first, then and finally.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner what Abraham said when the star disappeared. The partner says it back.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentences about the moon. Listener notes Abraham’s question. Writer writes his answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Do you like to look at the sky at night?” The learner answers and links it to Abraham.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Abraham was in search of one true Creator.” into their home language. How does their home language say “in search of”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham saw in the night sky. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Abraham asks ‘Could this be my Lord?’ two times. Why does the writer repeat the question?” (It shows his search step by step.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The events are in the right order. Learners say why the star and the moon could not be his Lord.

objectives: Explain what the sun helped Abraham understand: Allah is the Creator and the sun is a creation.
Follow the order: night → morning → sunset → prayer → duty → words to his father.
Discover what “had to” means, and use time words (all night, In the morning, When), If + present … will …, and Stop + -ing.
Talk about a duty and give one polite instruction.
content.pedagogy: Build a timeline across the board from night to morning to evening and add the prayer and the new duty. Learners place a sentence from the text on each point. Then you ask “Was guiding his people a choice or his job now?” and learners discover the meaning of “had to”. The prayer sentence is read and explained, never changed; the error-correction activity only uses the sentence in the app.
priorKnowledge: Morning, night, sun; “have to” in the present; the star-and-moon pattern from Chapter 3.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners say the sun is “bad”; the text says the sun is a creation and Allah is the Creator.
After “If”, learners use “will” (*If Allah will not show …).
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: had to + base verb (a duty in the past) · time words: all night, In the morning, When · If + present, … will … · Stop + -ing · imperatives: Follow me.
Notice (Activity 1): Board “From then on, he had to guide his people.” Ask: “Was this a choice or his job now? Why?” Learners connect it with “Allah … made him His Messenger.”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete the time words, then correct “If Allah will not show …” and “Stop worship stones.” Ask: “Where does ‘will’ go: in the If part or in the result part?”
Likely errors: *If Allah will not show · *Stop worship / *Stop to worship · *on the morning · *had to guided.
Use (Activity 4): three sentences about school or home: If I don’t …, I will … . I have to … . Stop …-ing / Please …!
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause between the two parts: “If alLAH DOESn’t SHOW me the RIGHT WAY, | I will be on the WRONG PATH.”
Contrastive stress: “alLAH is the creATor | … not a creAtion.”
“had to” is /hæd tə/ or /hættə/: “he HAD to GUIDE his PEOple.”
Word focus: cre-A-tion, cre-A-tor, FORE-head, PRAYER (one syllable), MES-sen-ger.
beforeReading: Recall Chapter 3 in one minute: What happened to the star and the moon? Then ask: “What comes after the night?”
duringReading: Put the events on the timeline: All night → morning → sunset → prayer → Messenger → father.
Underline the sentence about what Abraham understood when the sun set.
Box the sentence with “had to”.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (why the bright sun was not Allah).
Language Focus: Discover “had to” (Activity 1), practise time words and correct the if-sentence and Stop + -ing (Activities 2–3), then use condition, duty and instruction (Activity 4).
Write one sentence about a duty you have at home or at school.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 One-minute recall of the star and the moon, then “What comes after the night?”; 4–11 Listen and read; 11–18 Timeline on the board: Groups of four get one event card each and put it in the right place with a sentence from the text; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (choice or duty?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 on the board with learners explaining each correction; 31–37 Use: “Class duties” in pairs, each learner says one “If I don’t …, I will …” and one “I have to …” sentence, then writes one polite instruction for the class door (Please stop running in the corridor!); 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did the sun help Abraham understand?
What did Abraham ask for in his prayer?
What was Abraham’s new duty?
interactiveTips: Use The Setting Sun hotspot for the Creator/creation idea and the Prayer hotspot for Abraham’s words to Allah.
Replay the prayer sentence once, calmly, and ask what Abraham was afraid of.
The prayer is read and explained; learners do not rewrite or act it out.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “In the morning, ____. When the sun set, he understood that ____. He had to ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about a school duty with If … will …, have to, Stop + -ing and one polite imperative.

formativeAssessment: States the Creator/creation idea correctly.
Explains “had to” as a duty.
Keeps “will” out of the If part and uses Stop + -ing.
expectedResponses: When the sun set, Abraham understood that Allah is not a creation but the Creator of everything; Allah made him His Messenger, so he had to guide his people.
content.transferTask: Say what you have to do at home this week and give one polite instruction to a classmate.
content.teacherReflection: Did the timeline keep the order of the chapter clear, and did learners discover the meaning of “had to” from the story sentence?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups of four, each person gets one event card. Put your card in the right place on the board timeline and read your sentence from the story.
checkQuestions: How many cards does each person get? (one)
What do you read? (the sentence from the story)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that the sunset card comes before the card about Abraham becoming a Messenger. In Activity 3, ask learners to explain each correction aloud. In Class duties, listen for no “will” in the If part.

exitTicket: Complete: “If I don’t ____, I will ____. At home I have to ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Says Allah is the Creator and not a creation.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the sentence after the sunset.

rubricLevels.secure: Puts the events in order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last cards.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses had to, If … will and Stop + -ing correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each pattern.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes one duty and one polite instruction for the class.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “Please stop …ing in the corridor!”.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham prays and accepts a duty. Daily times of the day (night, morning, sunset) organise life in many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: In Türkiye, the call to prayer and sunset (iftar in Ramadan) mark the day. What marks the day in an English town (church bells, school bells, the five o'clock news, tea time)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners compare routines with respect. A routine that looks unusual to an outsider has meaning for the people who keep it.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note the sun, Abraham’s prayer and what he told his father.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners say three things Abraham understood about Allah.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner what Abraham told his father. The partner says how his father felt.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Questioner asks “What did Abraham ask Allah?”. Finder reads the answer sentence. Summarizer says it in his or her own words.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “How do you speak to a parent when you disagree?” The learner answers and links it to Abraham.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He never leaves us alone.” into their home language. Did each pair keep the word “never”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham understood when the sun set. Next lesson ask what their listener said.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The sun is ‘bigger and brighter’. Why does the writer put the sun last?” (Even the biggest thing in the sky is not the Creator.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners keep the creation and the Creator apart. The notes give the father’s question.

objectives: Say what Abraham told his people and what reason the people gave.
Tell the difference between “our fathers did it” and a real reason about power to help.

Understand key phrases (Leave here now, bow down to, heals me, didn’t listen to him), use do / do not / have with I, you, they and plural nouns, and use “when + present” for something that happens every time.
State an opinion with “I believe … because …” about an everyday topic.
content.pedagogy: Make a “Who said it?” card sort: Sentences from the father, from Abraham and from the people. Learners sort them and underline the reason each speaker gives. The language comes from the talk itself: Learners notice that Abraham says “I do not worship”, “Why do you …?” and “Your gods have …”, and they work out when we use do/does and have/has before you confirm it.
priorKnowledge: Present simple with I / you / he; food, drink, sick.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “Leave here now” is the father’s answer from the end of Chapter 4, not Abraham’s words.
Learners think “didn’t listen” means the people did not hear; they heard him but did not accept his words.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: meaning of key phrases (Leave here now, bow down to, heals me, didn’t listen to him) · I / you / they / plural nouns + do not, do, have (he / she / it + does, has) · when + present = every time · have no power to + verb · because.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match the four phrases with their meanings. Then ask: “Did the people hear Abraham? Did they listen to him? What is the difference?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose “do not”, “do” and “have”, then build “My Lord gives me food and drink when I need them.” and find the twin sentence “He heals me when I am sick.”
Likely errors: *I does not · *Why does you …? · *Your gods has · *when I will need.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about everyday life: I believe … because … . When I am tired, I … . My phone has / has no power to … .
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress: “I beLIEVE in alLAH. | I do NOT WORship stone IDols.”
Weak “do” in questions: “WHY do you BOW DOWN to these OBjects?” /duː/ → /də/.
-s endings: gives /z/, heals /z/, needs /z/.
Sentence stress: “They have NO POWer to HELP you.”
Word focus: be-LIEVE, POW-er, HEALS, KING-dom.
beforeReading: Ask: “If everybody in your family does something, is that a reason to do it? Is it proof?” Take two short answers and keep the question open.
duringReading: Listen: Who speaks first? (the father)
Card sort in pairs: father / Abraham / the people.
Underline the people’s reason and Abraham’s three examples (food and drink, healing, no power).
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (the people’s real reason).
Language Focus: Match the phrases (Activity 1), practise do / have (Activity 2), build the “when” sentence (Activity 3), then state a belief, a reason and a routine (Activity 4).
Give one opinion about school life with “I believe … because …”.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Question: Is “everybody in my family does it” a proof?; 4–10 Listen (Who speaks first?) and read along; 10–17 “Who said it?” card sort in pairs with six sentences, then learners read one card each aloud; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 with the question “hear or listen?”, Activity 2 individually with a pair check (Why do and not does?), Activity 3 as a board build; 30–37 Use: Opinion line, learners stand on the “agree” or “disagree” side of the room for statements such as “Breakfast is important” and give one “I believe … because …” sentence, then write it with one “When …” sentence; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What reason did the people give for bowing down to the idols?
What does Abraham say Allah does for him?
Did the people hear Abraham? Did they listen to him?
interactiveTips: Use the One God hotspot for the people’s reason and the Allah Provides hotspot for food, drink and healing.
Replay the father’s words at the start so learners know who is speaking.
Opinion statements in the Use step are everyday topics, not beliefs of classmates.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “I believe ____ because ____. When I am ____, I ____.” Give a do/does and have/has table.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a helpful person or thing: What it does when you need it and what it has no power to do.

formativeAssessment: Separates the people’s reason (their fathers) from Abraham’s examples.
Uses do / have with I, you, they and plural nouns.
Uses “when + present” for something that happens every time.
expectedResponses: The people said they worshipped the idols because they saw their fathers do it; Abraham said Allah gives him food and drink and heals him, and the idols have no power to do these things.
content.transferTask: Give one opinion about school life with “I believe … because …” and one routine with “When …”.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the difference between following a habit and giving a reason, and did they correct do/does themselves?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, sort the six cards: who said each sentence, Abraham or the people? Then read one card each aloud.
checkQuestions: How many cards? (six)
What do you decide for each card? (who said it)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “we saw our fathers do it” goes to the people. Listen in Activity 2 for “do” with they. On the opinion line, make sure each learner gives a reason with because.

exitTicket: Complete: “I believe ____ because ____. When I need help, ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Separates the people’s reason from Abraham’s examples.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who talks about their fathers?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses key phrases such as gives me food and drink and heals me.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the phrases in the text.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses do and have with I, you, they and plural nouns.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give “they do / they does” and ask which is right.

rubricLevels.secure: Says one opinion with I believe … because … and one when sentence.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frames on the board.

interculturalFocus.notice: The people say 'our fathers did it' to explain their custom. Every culture has traditions people keep because their parents did.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Name one tradition you keep because your family keeps it (a holiday meal, kissing hands at Bayram). Can you explain its reason in English?
interculturalFocus.perspective: The chapter questions one tradition, not all traditions. Learners notice the difference between a custom with a reason and one kept without thinking.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note what Abraham said to the people and what they answered.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners compare in two sentences: “The people said …” and “But Abraham said …”.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner why the people worshipped the idols. The partner says what Abraham answered.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads Abraham’s last words. Listener holds up one finger for each thing Allah does. Writer writes them.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Do people always do what their parents did?” The learner answers and links it to the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “But people didn’t listen to him.” into their home language. How does their home language say “listen to”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why the people did not listen to Abraham. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends with ‘But people didn’t listen to him.’ Why is this short sentence important?” (It shows that Abraham needs a new way.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners keep the two reasons apart. The notes give two things Allah does.

objectives: Retell Abraham’s plan step by step.
Say what Abraham wanted to show his people.
Discover what “is getting cold” means, and use wanted to + verb, did not tell anyone, There was / There were, and sequence words (When …, began to, one after another, In the end).
Describe a simple, harmless plan for a class event in order.
content.pedagogy: Order is the key to this chapter. Groups receive the five sequencing sentences on paper strips and put them in order before they open Activity 3 in the app. The language work starts with Abraham’s joke: You ask “Is the food cold now, or is it changing?” and learners discover that “is getting + adjective” shows a change happening now.
priorKnowledge: Simple past verbs, “There is / There are” in the present.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners think the largest idol was left because it was stronger; the chapter does not say why, and Chapter 7 shows the reason. Keep it as an open question.
Learners use “There was” with plural nouns (*There was plates).
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: is getting + adjective (becoming) · wanted to + verb · did not tell anyone · There was (one thing) / There were (more than one) · sequence: When …, began to …, one after another, In the end.
Notice (Activity 1): Board “Why don’t you eat the food? It is getting cold.” Ask: “Is the food cold now, or is it changing? Why is Abraham joking?” Learners explain that the idols cannot eat.
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose “to show”, “anyone” and “were”, then order the steps of the plan and circle the words that help (When, began to, one after another, In the end).
Likely errors: *wanted show · *did not tell nobody · *There was plates · *began break.
Use (Activity 4): four or five sentences about a plan for a class event (a surprise for a teacher, a class party): We wanted to … We made a plan to … There was / were … When … , we began to … In the end, … .
content.pronunciationFocus:
Linking: “one after another” sounds like one word: /wʌn ɑːftər əˈnʌðə/.
-ed endings: wanted /ɪd/, waited /ɪd/, placed /t/, hurried /d/.
Question with a smile, not a shout: “WHY DON’T you EAT the FOOD? | It is GETting COLD.”
Word focus: FES-ti-val, un-BRO-ken, JOK-ing-ly, HUR-ried, AXE.
beforeReading: Show the word “festival”. Ask: “When there is a big festival, where do people go? What is the town like?” Collect “empty, quiet” as predictions.
duringReading: Listen and count the steps of the plan on your fingers.
Underline what Abraham wanted to show his people.
Circle When, began to, one after another and In the end.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (when Abraham went into the house of the idols).
Language Focus: Discover “is getting cold” (Activity 1), practise the plan and scene words (Activity 2), order the steps (Activity 3), then describe a simple plan (Activity 4).
Keep “Why did he leave the largest one?” open for Chapter 7.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Festival prediction: What is a town like during a big festival?; 4–10 Listen and count the steps, then read; 10–17 Strip race in groups of four: Five paper strips from the chapter, groups put them in order and read them aloud, the first correct group explains one sequence word; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (cold now or changing?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 quickly because the strips were already ordered; 30–37 Use: Groups plan a surprise for a teacher or a class party and write four or five sentences with wanted to, There was / were, When, began to and In the end, one group reads; 37–40 Exit ticket plus the open question: Why did he leave the largest one?
discussionPoints: What did Abraham want to show his people?
Why was the festival a good time for the plan?
What did Abraham do with the axe at the end?
interactiveTips: Use The Axe hotspot for the end of the plan and The Largest Idol hotspot for the scene in the big house.
Replay “Why don’t you eat the food? It is getting cold.” and ask whether Abraham is serious or joking.
Do not act out breaking; the order task is done with strips and words.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the five steps with the first word of each missing (He got / When / began / In the end / placed) and the frame “There was ____. There were ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences about a class plan with five different sequence words and one “is getting + adjective” sentence.

formativeAssessment: Puts the steps in the right order.
Explains “is getting cold” as a change.
Uses There was / There were and wanted to + verb correctly.
expectedResponses: Abraham wanted to show his people that it was silly to love and talk to idols; when the town was empty, he broke the stone gods one after another, left the largest one unbroken and placed the axe around its neck.
content.transferTask: Describe a harmless plan for a class event in four or five ordered sentences.
content.teacherReflection: Did the strip race make the order clear, and did learners keep the question about the largest idol open without inventing a reason?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups of four, put the five strips in order. Read them aloud. The first correct group explains one sequence word.
checkQuestions: How many strips? (five)
What does the first correct group do? (explains one sequence word)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “left the largest one unbroken” comes after the breaking. Listen for “is getting cold” as a change. In the surprise plan, check for There was or There were.

rubric: There was / were, wanted to, is getting
exitTicket: Complete: “We wanted to ____. There were ____. In the end, ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Puts the steps in the right order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the first and last strips.

rubricLevels.secure: Says why Abraham made the plan.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “What did he want to show his people?”.

rubricLevels.criterion: There was / were, wanted to, is getting
rubricLevels.secure: Uses There was or There were, wanted to and is getting correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes an ordered plan with When and In the end.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the four sentence starters.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham uses the day of a festival when people leave the town.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: What happens in your town during a festival or Bayram (people visit family, streets are quiet or very busy)? Is it the same in an English-speaking town at Christmas or Thanksgiving?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Describe festivals with facts learners know. Avoid comparing whose festival is better.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note Abraham’s plan and what he did.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners tell the chapter in four steps.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner where Abraham put the axe. The partner guesses why.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Finder finds Abraham’s joke. Reader reads it aloud. Explainer says why it is a joke.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “Is there a big festival in your town?” The learner describes it in two sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “When the town was empty, he went into the big house full of human-like objects.” into their home language. Which word did each pair choose for “empty”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham did when the town was empty. Next lesson ask what their listener guessed about the axe.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer tell us that Abraham left the largest idol unbroken?” (It prepares his answer in the next chapter.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The steps are in the right order. The retell says that he left the largest idol.

objectives: Say what the people found and what they admitted about their idols.
Explain how Abraham’s questions make the people think.

Discover the difference between question-word questions (Who? Why?) and yes/no questions (Did …? Don’t you …? Are you …?), and use The next day, shocked because, displeased with, Did + base verb, can + base verb and plural + don’t.
Ask and answer questions about a harmless classroom mystery.
content.pedagogy: This chapter is built from questions. Learners hunt for every question in the text and write each one on a sticky note or in their notebooks. Then they sort them: “Can you answer it with yes or no?” They discover that Who? and Why? ask for information, while Abraham’s yes/no questions make the people see something they already know.
priorKnowledge: Question words who, why; “Did you …?” in the past; “can / can’t”.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners think the people accepted Abraham’s message when they said “these objects don’t speak”; they only admitted a fact.
Learners think the biggest idol really broke the others; Abraham said it to make them say that idols cannot speak.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: question-word questions (Who …? Why …?) vs yes/no questions (Did …? Don’t you …? Are you …?) · The next day · shocked because … · displeased with · Did + base verb · can + base verb · plural subject + don’t.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort four questions. Ask: “Which questions can you answer with yes or no? Abraham asks ‘Don’t you see …?’ Do the people know the answer?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete The next day / shocked / with, then correct “Did you harmed”, “can speaks” and “these objects doesn’t speak”.
Likely errors: *Did you harmed · *can speaks · *these objects doesn’t speak · *displeased of.
Use (Activity 4): four or five lines about a harmless classroom mystery (Who moved my bag?): The next day … Who …? Did you …? I know that … It can’t … because … .
content.pronunciationFocus:
Wh- questions fall: “WHO did THIS?↘” / “WHY do you WORship these OBjects?↘”
Yes/no questions rise: “Did you HARM our GODS?↗” / “Are you CRAzy?↗” (read calmly, not as an insult).
-ed endings: shocked /t/, asked /t/, wondered /d/, remembered /d/, displeased /d/.
Word focus: dis-PLEASED, pro-TECT, them-SELVES, WON-dered, CALM-ly (silent l).
beforeReading: Recall the end of Chapter 6: what did Abraham leave, and where did he put the axe? Ask: “What will the people say the next day?”
duringReading: Listen: How did the people feel? (shocked, displeased)
Question hunt: Copy every question in the chapter.
Underline the people’s answer that helps Abraham: “You know that these objects don’t speak!”
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (why Abraham said “Ask it if it can speak!”).
Language Focus: Sort the questions (Activity 1), practise time and feeling words (Activity 2), correct the verbs (Activity 3), then ask and explain (Activity 4).
Play a short “classroom mystery” question game.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Recall the axe and the largest idol, predict the people’s first question; 4–10 Listen (How did they feel?) and read along; 10–17 Question hunt in pairs: Copy all the questions, then answer: Who asks it? Does it need yes/no?; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Do the people know the answer?), Activities 2–3 in pairs, then learners say each corrected sentence aloud; 30–37 Use: “Classroom mystery” game, you hide a pen, learners ask Did you …? / Who …? / Can it …? questions and a partner answers, then each pair writes four lines; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why were the people shocked?
What did the people say about the idols that helped Abraham?
Did saying “these objects don’t speak” change the people’s minds?
interactiveTips: Use the Broken Idols hotspot for the scene and the Abraham’s Answer hotspot for Abraham’s answer and questions.
Replay the questions and ask learners to show a rising or falling hand for the intonation.
Abraham’s “Don’t you understand?” is part of the story; in class dialogues learners use polite questions.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a two-column table (Who / Why questions | Did / Are / Don’t questions) and the frames “Did you ____? I know that ____. It can’t ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a six-line dialogue about a classroom mystery with two question-word questions, two yes/no questions and one “because”.

formativeAssessment: Sorts questions by type and says what each asks for.
Uses the base verb after Did and can.
Explains that the people admitted a fact but did not change their belief.
expectedResponses: The people said, “You know that these objects don’t speak!” so Abraham asked why they worshipped objects that cannot speak, see or even protect themselves.
content.transferTask: Ask and answer four polite questions about a small classroom mystery.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use questions for their meaning (asking for a person, a reason, or making someone think) and not only for their form?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, copy all the questions in the chapter. For each one, write who asks it and if it needs a yes or no answer.
checkQuestions: What do you copy? (all the questions)
What two things do you write for each? (who asks it, yes/no or not)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that pairs find the people’s admission “these objects don’t speak”. In the Classroom mystery game, listen for the base verb after Did. Help pairs who answer a Who question with yes or no.

exitTicket: Write one “Who …?” question and one “Did you …?” question about yesterday.

rubricLevels.secure: Gives the people’s admission from the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the sentence with “You know that …”.

rubricLevels.secure: Sorts yes/no questions and wh-questions.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Can you answer this with yes or no?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses the base verb after Did and can, and don’t correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Write “Did you broke / Did you break” and ask which is right.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a short polite dialogue with four lines.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the question words on cards.

interculturalFocus.notice: The people are shocked and ask questions. How people ask questions politely differs across languages.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: In Turkish we can ask 'Bunu kim yaptı?' quite directly. Which English forms are more polite (Do you know who …? Could you tell me …?)
interculturalFocus.perspective: Directness is not rudeness in every culture. Learners practise one direct and one softer English question and choose which fits a teacher or a friend.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note what the people found and what Abraham said.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners act the scene in the house of idols in four lines.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner Abraham’s answer about the biggest idol. The partner says why the people were displeased.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Questioner asks “Why did Abraham say the biggest idol did it?”. Finder reads his questions. Summarizer explains them.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “How do you show someone a mistake without anger?” The learner answers and links it to Abraham’s calm words.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “It was this god there, the biggest one.” into their home language. How did each pair say “the biggest one”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Abraham answered the people. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener said.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Abraham asks three questions at the end. Why does the writer end the chapter with questions?” (They make the people and the reader think.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The scene keeps the facts of the chapter. Learners say why Abraham’s answer was clever.

content.chapter: Chapter 8 — Abraham Is Thrown into the Fire
objectives: Describe the danger of the fire with two details from the text, calmly and without extra detail.
Explain why Abraham stayed calm: He trusted Allah.
Discover what “too + adjective + to” means, and use so + adjective + that, to + verb for purpose, could not + verb, felt ashamed, stayed calm and finally.
Describe a safe everyday situation with too … to and so … that.
content.pedagogy: Keep the tone calm: You read the chapter once with the audio, without dramatic voices. Learners build two lists: “The people” (ashamed, arrogant, shouting, collecting firewood) and “Abraham” (calm, trusted Allah). The grammar starts with one question: “Did the people accept their mistake?” Learners discover that “too arrogant to accept” means that their arrogance stopped them.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners say “too” means “very”; in the text it shows that something stopped an action.
Learners jump to the result of Chapter 9; in Chapter 8 Abraham is calm because he trusted Allah, not because he knew what would happen.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: too + adjective + to + verb (it stops an action) · so + adjective + that (a result) · to + verb for purpose (came to watch) · could not + verb · feelings and actions: Felt ashamed, stayed calm, collected, finally.
Notice (Activity 1): Board “But they were too arrogant to accept their mistake.” Ask: “Did the people accept their mistake? Which word tells you?” Then compare with “The fire was so huge that it was dangerous to go near it.”: “Which sentence tells us a result?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose so / to watch / could not, then match felt ashamed, stayed calm, collected and finally with their meanings.
Likely errors: *too arrogant for accept · *very huge that · *came for watch · *could not flew.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a safe everyday situation (a very hot day, a heavy school bag): The bag was too heavy to … . The sun was so hot that … . We went to the park to … . Finally, … .
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the result: “The FIRE was SO HUGE | that it was DANgerous | to go NEAR it.”
“too” is stressed, “to” is weak: “TOO ARrogant | tə acCEPT their misTAKE”.
Read the people’s shouting in a normal, calm voice; do not ask learners to shout it.
-ed endings: collected /ɪd/, trusted /ɪd/, traveled /d/, tied /d/, placed /t/.
Word focus: AR-ro-gant, CAT-a-pult, DAN-ger-ous, a-SHAMED, FI-nal-ly.
beforeReading: Recall the end of Chapter 7 in one sentence. Tell learners that the chapter is serious and we read it calmly. Preview “calm” and “trusted” with a picture of a calm face.
duringReading: Listen once with the audio: How did the people feel? how did Abraham feel?
Two lists: The people / Abraham, with words from the text.
Underline two sentences that show how big and hot the fire was.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (calm in danger).
Language Focus: Discover “too … to” (Activity 1), practise so … that, purpose and could not (Activity 2), match feeling and action words (Activity 3), then describe a safe situation (Activity 4).
Write one sentence about a time you stayed calm.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Recall Chapter 7 and preview “calm” and “trusted”; 4–10 Listen once with the audio in a calm voice, then read silently; 10–16 Two lists in pairs (The people / Abraham), each with words from the text, whole-class check; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–29 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (Did they accept it?), Activity 2 individually, Activity 3 in pairs; 29–36 Use: “Too or so?” picture game, you show or describe a heavy bag, a hot drink, a long queue, pairs say one too … to and one so … that sentence, then write four sentences about a safe everyday situation; 36–40 Exit ticket: One sentence about a time you stayed calm.
discussionPoints: Why did the people feel ashamed?
What stopped them from accepting their mistake?
Why did Abraham stay calm?
interactiveTips: Use The Fire hotspot for the size of the fire and The Catapult hotspot only to explain the word.
Do not preview the result of Chapter 9.
No acting, drawing or sound effects of the fire or the throwing.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “They were too ____ to ____. The fire was so ____ that ____. Abraham stayed calm because ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a safe everyday situation with too … to, so … that, to + verb, could not and finally.

formativeAssessment: Gives two danger details from the text without extra detail.
Explains “too … to” as something that stops an action.
States the reason for Abraham’s calm from the text.
expectedResponses: The people were too arrogant to accept their mistake; the fire was so huge that it was dangerous to go near it, but Abraham stayed calm because he trusted Allah.
content.transferTask: Describe a safe everyday situation (a hot day, a heavy bag) with too … to and so … that.
content.teacherReflection: Was the chapter read calmly and without drama, and did learners find the meaning of “too … to” from the story sentence?

classroomManagement.instructions: Read the chapter quietly. With your partner, make two lists: the people and Abraham. Use words from the story.
checkQuestions: How many lists? (two)
Whose words do you use? (the story’s words)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Keep the reading calm. Check that the danger details are from the text only. In the Too or so game, listen for “too … to” and “so … that”. Check that the Use situations are safe and everyday.

exitTicket: Complete: “My bag was too heavy to ____. The day was so hot that ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Gives two danger details from the text without extra detail.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the two sentences about the fire.

rubricLevels.secure: Says Abraham stayed calm because he trusted Allah.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Why was he calm?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses too … to, so … that and to + verb for purpose.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one example of each to copy and change.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes about a time he or she stayed calm.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the frame “I stayed calm when …”.

interculturalFocus.notice: The people feel ashamed but cannot accept their mistake. Ideas about 'saving face' exist in many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Is it easy to say 'I was wrong' in public in Turkish culture? Is it easier or harder in other cultures you know (for example, in Japan, where 'face' is very important)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Keep this chapter calm and short. Learners talk about pride in general, not about real people in their class.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note how the people felt and what they prepared.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners say two sentences: one about the people and one about Abraham.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner why Abraham stayed calm. The partner says it back with “because”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentences about the fire. Listener notes how big it was. Writer writes two details.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “What helps you stay calm when you are afraid?” The learner answers and links it to Abraham.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “But Abraham (pbuh) stayed calm because he trusted Allah.” into their home language. How did each pair say “stayed calm”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why Abraham stayed calm. Next lesson ask what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer explains what a catapult is. Why does the writer add this?” (Some readers do not know the word.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners say that the people knew Abraham was right. The retell names the catapult.

objectives: Say what changed in the fire and what did not change in the people.
Explain Abraham’s answer to Gabriel with the text.
Discover what “not … at all” adds, and use became + adjective, turned into + noun, still, anything in questions and nothing = not anything.
Describe a surprising change where one thing still stayed the same.
content.pedagogy: Use a “changed / did not change” board. Learners put the fire, the ropes, Abraham and the people in the right column with a sentence from the text. The language grows from this: Learners discover that became and turned into show a change, and still shows that the people did not change. The miracle is read with respect; learners explain it, they do not act it out.
priorKnowledge: The danger and Abraham’s calm from Chapter 8; “something / anything / nothing”.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners think the people changed their belief because they were amazed; the text says “they did not change their minds”.
“Nothing from you!” is read as “I have nothing”; it means “I do not want anything from you”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: not … at all (a stronger negative) · became + adjective / turned into + noun (a change) · still (no change) · anything in questions / nothing = not anything · but (contrast).
Notice (Activity 1): Board “People were shocked to see that Abraham (pbuh) was not harmed at all.” Ask: “Did the fire hurt him a little? What do the words ‘at all’ add?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete became / turned into / still, then choose the meaning of “Nothing from you!”
Likely errors: *turned into cool (use became + adjective) · *they still were against him (still after “were”) · “Nothing from you” read as “I have nothing”.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a surprising change (a classroom that turned into a museum, a rainy day that became sunny): … became … / … turned into … / but … still … .
content.pronunciationFocus:
Linking: “not HARMED at ALL” sounds like /nɒt hɑːmd ə tɔːl/.
Contrastive stress: “The MIRacle aMAZED the PEOple, | but they did NOT CHANGE their MINDS.”
Question rises, answer falls: “Is there ANYthing you WISH for?↗” / “NOTHing from YOU!↘”
-ed endings: harmed /d/, amazed /d/, turned /d/, cooled /d/.
Word focus: MIR-a-cle, a-MAZED, GA-bri-el, CON-di-tion.
beforeReading: Retrieve the end of Chapter 8 in one sentence (Abraham was thrown into the fire). Ask: “What do you think happened next?” and keep the answers as predictions.
duringReading: Listen for gist: What did Gabriel ask, and what did Abraham answer?
Two columns: changed / did not change, each with a sentence from the text.
Underline “still” twice.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (what happened in the fire).
Language Focus: Discover “not … at all” (Activity 1), practise became / turned into / still (Activity 2), understand “Nothing from you!” (Activity 3), then describe a change (Activity 4).
Write one “… changed, but … still …” sentence about your own life.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Retrieve Chapter 8 and predict; 4–10 Listen for Gabriel’s question and Abraham’s answer, then read along; 10–17 Changed / did not change board: Pairs get four cards (the fire, the ropes, Abraham, the people) and place them with a sentence from the text; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (a little or not at all?), Activity 2 in pairs, Activity 3 with a quick hands-up vote before checking; 30–37 Use: Think-pair-share about a surprising change in their own life (a new school, a new sport), pairs write four sentences with became or turned into and still; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did the fire become for Abraham?
What did the fire burn?
Did the people change their minds after the miracle? Which word shows this?
interactiveTips: Use The Miracle hotspot for the change of the fire and the Angel Gabriel hotspot for the question and the answer.
Replay “… but they did not change their minds. They were still arrogant and rude.”
The miracle is explained with the text only; no acting or drawing of Abraham or the angel.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “The fire became ____. The fire turned into ____. But the people were still ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a surprising change with became, turned into, still, not … at all and but.

formativeAssessment: Separates what changed (the fire) from what did not change (the people).
Explains “not … at all” and “Nothing from you!”.
Uses became + adjective and turned into + noun correctly.
expectedResponses: The fire became cool and safe and only burnt the ropes, so Abraham was not harmed at all; the miracle amazed the people, but they were still against him.
content.transferTask: Describe a surprising change in your life where one thing changed but another thing still stayed the same.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep “amazed” and “changed their minds” apart, and did they find the job of “still” themselves?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, place the four cards under “changed” or “did not change”. Add a sentence from the story to each card.
checkQuestions: How many cards? (four)
What are the two places? (changed, did not change)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check that “the people” goes under “did not change”. In Activity 3, look at the hands-up vote before you check. In the Use task, listen for became + adjective and turned into + noun.

rubric: Meaning of not … at all / nothing

rubricLevels.secure: Separates what changed from what did not change.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Did the people change their minds?”.

rubricLevels.criterion: Meaning of not … at all / nothing
rubricLevels.secure: Explains not … at all as zero.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Was he hurt a little or not at all?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses became, turned into and still correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give “became cool / turned into a garden” as models.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes about a surprising change in his or her life.
rubricLevels.notYet: Offer two examples: a new school, a new sport.

interculturalFocus.notice: The fire becomes cool and safe for Abraham. Fire appears in the stories and festivals of many cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: In Türkiye people jump over a small fire at Hıdırellez or Nevruz in some regions. Do English-speaking countries have fire customs (Bonfire Night in the UK)?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Learners keep the story and the customs separate. The comparison is about how cultures use fire, not about the miracle.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note what happened in the fire and how the people reacted.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners say the miracle in three sentences.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner Abraham’s answer to Angel Gabriel. The partner says why he answered like this.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Finder finds the sentence about the ropes. Reader reads it aloud. Explainer says what the fire burnt and what it did not burn.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Who do you trust most?” The learner answers and links it to Abraham’s trust in Allah.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “The fire turned into a garden.” into their home language. How does their home language say “turned into”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how Allah saved Abraham from the fire. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The people were amazed but did not change their minds. Why does the writer show both?” (A miracle does not change an arrogant heart.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The retell says that the fire burnt only the ropes. Learners keep the miracle and the people’s answer apart.

objectives: Say what Nimrod claimed and what question Abraham asked him.
Explain why Nimrod could not answer the question about the sun.
Understand key words (ordinary, Let him go, brings death, angrier), use the past forms heard, thought and wanted, and discover the pattern order + person + to + verb.
Test a claim in a harmless classroom game with “Can you …?” and “couldn’t”.
content.pedagogy: Use a three-box chart: Claim / Nimrod’s example / Abraham’s test. The part about the slaves is read once by you, briefly and calmly, and learners only note what Nimrod wanted to show. The focus is the test: Learners discover that a question about the sun is something only Allah can do, so Nimrod could not answer. The grammar comes from Nimrod’s first actions: he heard, he thought, so he wanted.
priorKnowledge: can / can’t, east and west, simple past.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners think Nimrod really could give life and death; the text shows he could not make the sun rise from the west.
Learners write *thinked and *heared.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: key words (ordinary, Let him go, brings death, angrier) · irregular past heard, thought and regular wanted · So for a result · order + person + to + verb · Can you …? / couldn’t.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match the four expressions. Then ask: “Nimrod was angry before. After Abraham’s question he was ‘angrier’. What does -er add?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Complete heard / thought / wanted (not *thinked), then build “He ordered his guards to bring two slaves.” Ask: “Who got the order? What must they do?”
Likely errors: *thinked / *heared · *ordered his guards bring · *Can you makes …? · Nimrod *can’t (present) instead of couldn’t.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a claim and a test (My friend thought he could … . I asked, “Can you …?” He couldn’t … . So …).
content.pronunciationFocus:
Contrastive stress: “alLAH makes the SUN RISE in the EAST. | Can YOU make the SUN rise from the WEST?↗”
can / can’t: “I CAN give LIFE” /kən/ vs “couldn’t” /ˈkʊdnt/.
-ed endings: called /d/, ordered /d/, killed /d/, wanted /ɪd/, asked /t/.
Read the slave sentences once in a quiet, even voice.
Word focus: OR-di-nar-y, NIM-rod, GUARDS, AN-gri-er, SLAVES.
beforeReading: Write “claim” and “test” on the board. Example: “I can speak five languages.” – “Can you say ‘thank you’ in all five?” Learners say which sentence is the claim and which is the test.
duringReading: Listen for gist: Who is Nimrod, and why did he want to meet Abraham?
Fill the three boxes: claim / example / test.
Underline the sentence that says why Nimrod could not do it.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (how Abraham answered Nimrod).
Language Focus: Match the key words (Activity 1), practise heard / thought / wanted (Activity 2), build the order sentence (Activity 3), then make a claim and a test (Activity 4).
Play a short “Can you …?” challenge game in pairs.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Claim or test? with the language example on the board; 4–10 Listen for gist, then you read the slave part once calmly while learners follow; 10–16 Three-box chart in pairs (claim / example / test) with sentences from the text, whole-class check; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–29 Language Focus: Activity 1 with the question about -er, Activity 2 individually, Activity 3 as a board build (Who got the order?); 29–36 Use: “Can you …?” challenge in pairs, one learner makes a harmless claim (I can say the months backwards), the partner tests it and they write four sentences with thought, Can you …?, couldn’t / could and So; 36–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did Nimrod claim?
What question did Abraham ask him?
Why couldn’t Nimrod answer?
interactiveTips: Use the Nimrod hotspot for his claim and The Sun from the West hotspot for Abraham’s test.
Replay only the sun question and Nimrod’s reaction.
Do not discuss or act out the killing; keep attention on the claim and the test.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “Nimrod said ____. Abraham asked, ‘Can you ____?’ Nimrod couldn’t ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a harmless claim and test with heard, thought, wanted, Can you …? and couldn’t.

formativeAssessment: Separates Nimrod’s claim from Abraham’s test.
Uses heard / thought / wanted correctly.
Builds order + person + to + verb.
expectedResponses: Nimrod claimed he could give life and death, but when Abraham asked him to make the sun rise from the west, he couldn’t because only Allah can make the sun rise in the east.
content.transferTask: Make a harmless claim and let a partner test it with “Can you …?”.
content.teacherReflection: Did the lesson stay on the reasoning (claim and test) and keep the violent detail short and calm?

classroomManagement.instructions: With your partner, make a chart with three boxes: claim, example, test. Write a sentence from the story in each box.
checkQuestions: How many boxes? (three)
What goes in the test box? (the sun from the west)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Read the slave part once yourself in a calm voice. Check that Nimrod’s claim and Abraham’s test are in different boxes. In the Can you challenge, keep claims harmless.

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “thought” and one “Can you …?” question for a friend.

rubricLevels.secure: Separates Nimrod’s claim from Abraham’s test.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who said this? Was it a claim or a test?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Says why Nimrod could not answer.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who can make the sun rise?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses past forms and order + person + to + verb.
rubricLevels.notYet: Build one sentence together on the board.

rubricLevels.secure: Writes a short claim-and-test exchange.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the four frames: thought, Can you, couldn’t, So.

interculturalFocus.notice: Nimrod claims great power. Rulers who called themselves gods or demanded worship appear in the history of several cultures.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: How do people talk to and about leaders in Türkiye, and in an English-speaking country (Mr President, Prime Minister, Your Majesty)? What do these titles show?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Nimrod is shown only as a symbol in the book's pictures. Learners discuss power, not real politicians of today.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note what Nimrod said and Abraham’s answers. Keep the tone calm.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners explain in two sentences why Nimrod could not answer.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner Abraham’s question about the sun. The partner says why Nimrod could not do it.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Questioner asks “Who is your God?”. Finder reads Abraham’s answer. Summarizer says it in his or her own words.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “What does a good leader do with power?” The learner gives two ideas and compares them with Nimrod.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Nimrod was the King of Babylon.” into their home language. How does their home language write the name “Babylon”?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what Abraham asked Nimrod about the sun. Next lesson ask what their listener said.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends with ‘This made Nimrod angrier.’ What does this short sentence show?” (Nimrod had no answer.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The retell is calm. Learners give Abraham’s question about the sun correctly.

objectives: Say who believed with Abraham and why he decided to leave Babylon.
Follow the journey from Babylon to the quiet valley near Safa and Marwah.
Sort journey phrases into “where or how” and “when or how long”, and use decided to, to + verb for purpose, ask + person + to, began and arrive at.
Describe a real journey of your own.
content.pedagogy: Draw a simple route on the board: Babylon → Syria and Palestine → a quiet valley near Safa and Marwah. Learners add the transport, the time words and the people (Sarah, Lot, Hagar, Ishmael) from the text. The grammar grows from the map: Learners discover that some phrases answer “Where? How?” and others answer “When? How long?” before they sort them in Activity 1.
priorKnowledge: Family words (wife, son), travel words (camel, long, hot) and from … to ….
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners mix up the people: Sarah and Lot believed in Babylon, Hagar and Ishmael come later in the journey.
The reason for leaving gets lost among the places: he left to tell people about Allah’s message.
content.grammarFocus:
