Targets: where or how (from … to …, on camels, near …) vs when or how long (During …, for a long time, Finally) · decided to + verb · to + verb for purpose · ask + person + to + verb · began (past of begin) · arrive at.
Notice (Activity 1): learners sort six phrases. Ask: “Which words tell us the start and the end of the road? Which words tell us about time?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose “to leave”, “to tell” and “to travel”, then correct “begun” and “arrived to”.
Likely errors: *decided leaving · *for tell · *asked him travel · *begun his journey · *arrived to.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a real journey (a holiday, a visit to grandparents): We decided to … We traveled from … to … by bus / on a train. During the journey, … Finally, we arrived at … .
content.pronunciationFocus:
Chunk the route: “He Traveled | from BABylon | to SYRia and PALestine | on CAMels.”
-ed endings: believed /d/, decided /ɪd/, traveled /d/, married /d/, named /d/, arrived /d/.
List intonation: “a LONG, ↗ HOT, ↗ and TIRing JOURney↘”.
Word focus: JOUR-ney, VAL-ley, TIR-ing, PAL-es-tine, MES-sage.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you need for a long journey?” Learners name three things. Then ask: “Why do people leave their home town?”
duringReading: Listen for gist: Why did Abraham leave Babylon?
Draw the route in your notebook with the places and the transport.
Write the names of the people next to the right part of the route.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (the order of the journey).
Language Focus: Sort the journey phrases (Activity 1), practise decided to / to + verb / asked … to (Activity 2), correct began and arrived at (Activity 3), then describe a journey (Activity 4).
Tell a partner about a real journey you made.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 What do you need for a long journey? Why do people leave home?; 4–10 Listen for the reason, then read along; 10–17 Route on the board: Learners come up in turns and add a place, the camels, a time word or a name from the text, the class checks each addition; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 in pairs using the board route, Activity 2 individually, Activity 3 as a whole-class correction; 30–37 Use: Learners draw a small map of a real trip and tell a partner with decided to, from … to, by / on, During, Finally … arrived at, then write four sentences; 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Who believed in Allah with Abraham in Babylon?
Why did Abraham decide to leave?
Where did the journey end in this chapter?
interactiveTips: Use The Journey hotspot for the route and the Safa and Marwah hotspot for the end of the chapter.
Replay the time words (So, During his journey, One day, Finally) before the Quick Challenge.
Keep the names on the board so learners do not mix up Sarah, Lot, Hagar and Ishmael.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “He decided to ____. He traveled from ____ to ____ on ____. Finally, they arrived at ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write six sentences about a real journey with decided to, from … to, During, for a long time, asked … to and arrived at.

formativeAssessment: States the reason for leaving from the text.
Sorts place and time phrases.
Uses decided to, asked … to and arrived at correctly.
expectedResponses: Only Sarah and Lot believed with Abraham, so he decided to leave Babylon to tell people about Allah’s message; he traveled on camels, and finally Abraham, Hagar and Ishmael arrived at a quiet valley near Safa and Marwah.
content.transferTask: Describe a real journey with a decision, a route, transport, time and arrival.
content.teacherReflection: Were the people, the purpose and the route all clear, and did learners discover the place/time difference themselves?

classroomManagement.instructions: Come to the board in turns. Add one thing to the route: a place, the camels, a time word or a name from the story. The class checks each addition.
checkQuestions: How many things do you add? (one)
Who checks it? (the class)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Check the places from the text: Babylon, Syria and Palestine, the valley near Safa and Marwah. In the Use task, listen for “arrived at” and “by” or “on” for transport. Look at the maps quickly before learners write.

rubric: decided to / asked … to / arrived at
exitTicket: Complete: “Last year we decided to ____. We traveled from ____ to ____. Finally, we arrived at ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Gives the reason for leaving from the text.
rubricLevels.notYet: Ask “Who believed with Abraham? Only who?”.

rubricLevels.secure: Names the people and the route in order.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the places on cards to put on a line.

rubricLevels.criterion: decided to / asked … to / arrived at
rubricLevels.secure: Uses decided to, asked … to and arrived at correctly.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give one gap sentence for each.

rubricLevels.secure: Tells about a real trip with four sentences.
rubricLevels.notYet: Give the journey frames on the board.

interculturalFocus.notice: Abraham, Sarah and Lot leave Babylon, in today's Iraq. Moving to a new land for one's beliefs or safety is part of many families' histories.
interculturalFocus.compare: Ask: Do you know families who moved from one city or country to another (internal migration in Türkiye, Turkish families in Germany)? What did they bring with them?
interculturalFocus.perspective: Some learners may have a family migration story; others may not want to share. Let them use a known historical example instead.

noteTaking.focus: While listening, learners note who believed and Abraham’s journey.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes, learners say the journey in four sentences.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner tells a partner why Abraham left Babylon. The partner says where he went.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 2. Listener notes the places. Writer writes them in order.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “Have you been on a long journey?” The learner answers and compares it with Abraham’s journey.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “It was a long, hot, and tiring journey.” into their home language. Which words did each pair choose for the three adjectives?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, where Abraham traveled after Babylon. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends with two hills, Safa and Marwah. Why does the writer name them?” (They are important in the next chapters.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The places are in the right order. The notes name Sarah, Lot, Hagar and Ishmael.

content.chapter: Chapter 12 — Hagar and Ishmael in the Valley
objectives: Describe what was missing in the valley.
Show how Hagar joined trust with action: She believed Allah would protect them and she searched for food and water.
Understand fearlessly, protect, blessings and useless, find where “never” goes with “will”, and use tell + person + to, had to and nobody.
Describe a need, a request, an action and a hope in a school situation.
content.pedagogy: Use two columns: “Hagar believed …” / “Hagar did …”. Learners fill both with sentences from the text and see that trust and effort go together. The language work starts with the words (Activity 1): you ask “Was Hagar afraid?” and learners find “fearlessly”. In Activity 2 they discover where “never” goes by building the sentence. The result of the search (Zamzam) is kept for Chapter 13.
priorKnowledge: food, water, hill, run, help; “will” for the future.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners think trust means doing nothing; Hagar looked for food and water and ran from hill to hill.
Learners tell the Zamzam result now; in Chapter 12 the search is still “useless”.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: key words (fearlessly, protect, blessings, useless) · will never / will (sure about the future) · let + person + base verb · tell + person + to + verb · had to (a duty in the past) · no … / nobody.
Notice (Activity 1): learners match the four words. Ask: “Was Hagar afraid? Which word tells you? Did running help her find water? Which word tells you?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Build “Allah will never let us die.” (Where does “never” go?), then choose “to stay”, “had to” and “nobody”.
Likely errors: *will not never · *let us to die · *told his wife stay · *must to give · *There was no water and anybody.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a school need (Our class had no … left. We had to … . We asked the teacher to … . I am sure it will …), not about death or danger.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Keep “never” strong: “alLAH will NEVer LET us DIE. | He will proTECT us.”
List intonation: “no FRUIT, ↗ no TREES, ↗ no FOOD, ↗ and no WAter↘”.
“had to” /hættə/, “nobody” /ˈnəʊbədi/.
-ed endings: asked /t/, looked /t/.
Word focus: FEAR-less-ly, BLESS-ings, USE-less, pro-TECT, PLAN-ner.
beforeReading: Ask: “What does a family need in an empty valley?” Pairs list four things; keep the list on the board.
duringReading: Listen and tick the things on our list that the valley did not have.
Two columns: Hagar believed … / Hagar did …
Underline what Abraham asked Allah for.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (why Hagar was not afraid).

Language Focus: Match the key words (Activity 1), build the “will never” sentence (Activity 2), practise told … to / had to / nobody (Activity 3), then describe need, request, action and hope (Activity 4).
Write one sentence about a time you tried hard and did not give up.
content.lessonPlan: 0–4 Pairs list what a family needs in an empty valley; 4–10 Listen and tick the missing things, then read along; 10–17 Stations: Four corners of the room with one question each (What was missing? What did Hagar believe? What did Hagar do? What did Abraham ask for?), groups move once and write one sentence from the text at each; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–30 Language Focus: Activity 1 with the questions “afraid?” and “did running help?”, Activity 2 as a board build, Activity 3 in pairs; 30–37 Use: Pairs imagine the class has run out of something for a project and write four sentences (no … left / had to / asked … to / will); 37–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What was missing in the valley?
What did Hagar believe?
What did Hagar do to find food and water?
interactiveTips: Use the Hagar’s Trust hotspot for her words and The Empty Valley hotspot for what was missing.
Replay Hagar’s words and ask: Does she sound afraid or sure?
Do not reveal the Zamzam water until Chapter 13.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Frames: “There was no ____. Hagar had to ____. She looked for ____. She believed Allah will ____.”
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write five sentences about a school need with no … left, had to, asked … to, nobody and will.

formativeAssessment: Joins Hagar’s trust with her actions.
Places “never” between “will” and the verb.
Uses told … to, had to and nobody correctly.
expectedResponses: Hagar believed Allah would protect them, and she also looked for food and water and ran from hill to hill, but there was no water and nobody to help her.
content.transferTask: Describe a school need: What was missing, what you had to do, what you asked for and what you hope.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see trust and effort together, and did I keep the Chapter 13 result for the next lesson?

classroomManagement.instructions: In groups, go to each corner of the room once. Answer the question there with one sentence from the story. Write your sentence on the sheet.
checkQuestions: How many corners do you visit? (four)
What do you write at each corner? (one sentence from the story)
classroomManagement.monitoring: Time each corner and give a clear signal to move. Check that groups join Hagar’s trust with her actions. In Activity 1, listen for the place of never: will never.

rubric: will never / told … to / had to / nobody
exitTicket: Complete: “We had no ____ left, so we had to ____. We asked ____ to ____.”

rubricLevels.secure: Names the missing things from the text.

objectives: Tell what was happening, what happened suddenly and what Hagar did next.
Follow the chain from the water to the city of Mecca.
Discover the difference between “was running” (going on) and “came” (one moment), and use Suddenly, became, because + sentence, because of + noun and imperatives (Flow slowly, stop!).

content.pedagogy: Tell learners to listen for one word: when they hear “Suddenly”, they raise a hand. This marks the turn in the chapter. Learners then draw a timeline with a long wavy line (was running, was crying) and a short arrow (water came out) and discover that “was + -ing” is the background and the past simple is the moment. The second paragraph becomes a cause-result chain: water → famous → people came → a city called Mecca.
priorKnowledge: Chapter 12: no water and nobody to help; simple past and “was / were”.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners think Mecca was already a city before the water; the text says people came because of the water and built a city.
Learners forget Hagar’s first actions: she shouted, drank and gave water to Ishmael.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: was / were + -ing (going on) vs past simple (one moment) · Suddenly · became (a change) · because + subject + verb vs because of + noun · imperatives: Flow slowly, stop!
Notice (Activity 1): Read “Hagar was running in the desert and Ishmael was crying for water. Suddenly water came out of the ground …” Ask: “What was happening when the water came? Which action was long, and which one was a moment?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Choose “became”, “because” and “because of”, then decide what the words “Flow” and “stop” do.
Likely errors: *Hagar running (no was) · *because this water · *because of it was a gift · *become for the past.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a sudden change in your life: I was … and my brother was … . Suddenly, … . Then, … because … .
content.pronunciationFocus:
Pause after “Suddenly”: “SUDdenly | WAter came OUT of the GROUND | under ISHmael’s FEET.”
Background sentences in an even voice: “HAgar was RUNning in the DEsert | and ISHmael was CRYing for WAter.”
Weak “of”: “because of this WAter” /bɪˈkɒz əv/.
Word focus: DES-ert (not des-SERT), SUD-den-ly, FA-mous, ZAM-zam, MEC-ca.
beforeReading: Retrieve the end of Chapter 12 (no water, nobody to help). Ask: “What do you think happened next?”

Draw the timeline: Wavy line for what was going on, arrow for the sudden event.
Number the chain in the second paragraph: water → famous → people came → city.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (why more people came).
Language Focus: Sort “going on” and “one moment” (Activity 1), practise became / because / because of (Activity 2), discover the imperatives (Activity 3), then tell a sudden change (Activity 4).
Tell a partner a short story from your life that has “Suddenly” in it.

Suddenly, …) and write four sentences, two volunteers read; 37–40 Exit ticket.

content.chapter: Chapter 14 — The Ka’ba and Abraham’s Message
objectives: Say what task Allah gave Abraham and how Ishmael answered.
Connect the Ka’ba, Hajj today and the final message as the chapter states them.
Discover that “will” can make a promise, see how one sentence answers When? Where? How often? Why?, and use After + past event, still and One of + plural.
Describe a shared class task with a promise, a purpose and something that continues.
content.pedagogy: This last chapter joins the story together. Start with a “story wall”: learners call out one word from each earlier chapter and you write them in a line on the board. Then learners read how the story ends: a task, a promise, a building, a place people still visit, and a message. The grammar starts with Ishmael’s answer: You ask “Is he talking about the past or the future? Is he sure?” and learners discover that “will … for sure” is a promise.
priorKnowledge: Mecca and Zamzam from Chapter 13; build, help, family.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Learners only remember the building and miss the final message.
Learners add details about the Ka’ba or Hajj that the text does not give; stay with the chapter’s sentences.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: will + verb for a promise · for sure (certainly) · one sentence that answers When? (During that time) Where? (Mecca) How often? (several times) Why? (to see his family) · After + past event · still (continues today) · One of + plural.
Notice (Activity 1): Board “Ishmael said, ‘I will help you for sure.’” Ask: “Is Ishmael talking about yesterday or about the future? Is he sure? Which words tell you?”
Build (Activities 2–3): Match the parts of “During that time, Abraham (pbuh) visited Mecca several times to see his family.” with When? / Where? / How often? / Why?, then complete After / still / One of.
Likely errors: *I help you for sure (no will) · *After Abraham builds · *people visit still · *One of them were.
Use (Activity 4): four sentences about a shared class task: Our class has an important job. My friend will help me for sure. We meet several times to … . After we finish, … still … .
content.pronunciationFocus:
Promise intonation: “I will HELP you | for SURE.↘”
Read the message slowly and calmly, with a pause at each full stop: “There is NO GOD but alLAH. | He has no PARTner | and He does not NEED any HELP.”
“One of them” links: /ˈwʌnəvðəm/.
Word focus: MIS-sion, u-NIQUE, PART-ner, SA-cred, SEV-er-al, KA’-ba, HAJJ.
beforeReading: Story wall: Learners call out one word for each chapter they remember (idols, father, star, sun …) and you write them in a line on the board. Ask: “How will the story end?”
duringReading: Listen for gist: What task did Allah give Abraham?
Underline Ishmael’s promise.
Box the sentence about today (people still visit …).
Read the final message and say it in your own words.
afterReading: Complete the Quick Challenge (the Ka’ba and the message).

Language Focus: Discover the promise (Activity 1), match the parts of the sentence with the questions (Activity 2), practise After / still / One of (Activity 3), then describe a shared task (Activity 4).
Then continue with the whole-book review: Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review, Master Glossary and the Final Challenge.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Story wall: One word from each chapter on the board, prediction of the ending; 5–12 Listen for the task, then read along; 12–18 Pairs complete a four-box chart (task / promise / today / message) with sentences from the text, whole-class check; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–31 Language Focus: Activity 1 as whole-class discovery (past or future? sure or not?), Activity 2 as a question game where you point to a part of the sentence and learners call out When?, Where?, How often? or Why?, Activity 3 in pairs; 31–37 Use: Groups choose a real shared class task (a class library, a clean-up day) and write four sentences with will … for sure, to + verb, After and still; 37–40 Exit ticket and a short preview of the whole-book review pages.
discussionPoints: What task did Allah give Abraham?
How did Ishmael answer his father?
What does the chapter say Hajj helps people remember?
What is Abraham’s message?
interactiveTips: Use the “Building the Ka’ba” hotspot for the building and the Hajj hotspot for the sentence about today.
The final message is read and explained, never gapped or changed.
Follow the real review order after this chapter: Knowledge Check → Vocabulary Challenge → Language Review → Master Glossary → Final Challenge.

metadata.title: Teacher Guide — Prophet Abraham (A2)
metadata.subtitle: TYMM-aligned guide with chapter-specific support, grammar discovered from the story and 40-minute lesson plans
metadata.estimatedDuration: 14 story chapters, one lesson of about 35–40 minutes each. The whole-book review pages (Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review, Master Glossary, Final Challenge) follow separately.
metadata.targetAudience: CEFR A2 English learners, especially middle-school students.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow short connected narratives with audio support, find a sentence in the text as evidence and produce short spoken or written answers with frames.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 listening, reading, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh), using the Quick Challenge and the Language Focus of every chapter, and turn the story’s values into small, observable actions without changing or extending the story.
metadata.approachDesc: Every chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading come first: learners understand the story and find a sentence as evidence; the Quick Challenge checks the key idea. Grammar is then learned inductively, as the Maarif Model expects for English: in the Language Focus, learners first LOOK at a form in a real story sentence and answer a simple meaning question (the rule is confirmed only after they say it in their own words), then PRACTISE it in short, meaningful tasks, and finally USE it in YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. At A2, steps are short, oral practice comes before writing and frames support every learner. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/yabanci-dil-alan-becerileri.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 14 Quick Challenges, evidence sentences, Language Focus tasks (Look → Practise → Use), short spoken and written transfer, exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and the Final Challenge.

formative: One Quick Challenge after every story chapter
Evidence checks (a sentence from the text)
Short spoken and written transfer about the learners’ own world

readingFramework.before: A short, chapter-specific hook: an object, a gesture, a question or a prediction about the next event.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist with one clear question, then read along and find sentences for the chapter’s key relationship: belief vs observation, habit vs event, question → conclusion, sequence, change vs no change, claim vs test, trust and action.
readingFramework.after: Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (Look → Practise → Use), then a short transfer about the learners’ own life and an exit ticket.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Prioritise the chapter’s Word Notes and only the words needed for the key relationship and the Language Focus.
vocabularyApproach.method: Guess meaning from the picture, the hotspot, the audio or the sentence before any definition.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse the words in the Use step, exit tickets and the whole-book review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask one simple meaning question (Were they real people? Is he sure? Did it happen one time or many times?), let learners say the rule in their own words, then confirm it briefly and practise it in context. At A2 keep grammar words to a minimum and use gestures, timelines and color. Do not replace the chapter work with unrelated grammar drills.
grammarSequence: Ch1: looked like; irregular past (grew, made, thought, saw, came); did not / could not + base verb
Ch2: again and again vs one time; used to + verb; bigger than; because; told … not to + verb
Ch3: Could this be …?; always thought about / wanted to know / was in search of; Then; because; could not be
Ch4: had to; all night / In the morning / When; If + present … will …; Stop + -ing
Ch5: key phrases (bow down to, heals me, didn’t listen to); do / do not / have with I, you, they; when + present
Ch6: is getting + adjective; wanted to; did not tell anyone; There was / There were; sequence words
Ch7: question-word vs yes/no questions; The next day; shocked because; displeased with; Did / can + base verb; plural + don’t
Ch8: too … to; so … that; to + verb for purpose; could not; felt ashamed / stayed calm / finally
Ch9: not … at all; became / turned into; still; anything / nothing
Ch10: ordinary / Let him go / angrier; heard, thought, wanted; order + person + to + verb
Ch11: place vs time phrases; decided to; to + verb for purpose; asked … to; began; arrive at
Ch12: fearlessly / blessings / useless; will never + verb; told … to; had to; nobody
Ch13: was + -ing vs past simple; Suddenly; became; because vs because of; imperatives
Ch14: will … for sure (promise); When? Where? How often? Why? in one sentence; After; still; One of

skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find a sentence as evidence, follow sequence, compare two sides and understand simple cause and result.
skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: listen for gist with one question, then replay a key sentence for detail and pronunciation.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: ask and answer questions, give reasons with because, retell short sequences and talk about the learners’ own life with frames.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write three to five connected A2 sentences using the chapter’s patterns and words.

valuesFocus: D6 Honesty — telling belief, claim and evidence apart and saying what the text really says
D10 Humility — the people were “too arrogant to accept their mistake”; accepting a mistake is a strength
D12 Patience — Abraham stayed calm and Hagar kept searching in difficulty
D16 Responsibility — Abraham “had to guide his people”; duties at home and at school
D20 Helpfulness — Ishmael: “I will help you for sure”; shared work
D14 Respect — discussing belief and difference respectfully, without mocking people
Values are chosen only where the chapter gives concrete support; see https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.
languageFocus: Every one of the 14 story chapters has an active Language Focus built as Look → Practise → Use.
Use the Language Focus after the story is understood and the Quick Challenge is done.
Always start from the story sentence: Ask what the form means before naming it.
Let learners answer first; the explanation shown after each answer confirms the rule they found.
At A2 the last step is short spoken or written production about the learners’ own world, prepared orally with a partner first.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce the language load, not the thinking: One evidence sentence at a time, frames, gestures, audio replay and oral practice before writing. Extend by adding one more chapter pattern or one more connected sentence, not by adding facts from outside the book.

sensitiveNotes.title: Respect and source fidelity
notes: Prophets and angels are never acted out, drawn or voiced by learners; dialogues are read by the teacher or the audio. Freeze-frames and role-plays use only everyday, non-story situations.
Qur’anic wording, prayers and the final message (“There is no god but Allah …”) are read, explained and matched to meanings; they are never gapped, corrected or rewritten.
The fire (Chapters 8–9), the father’s threat (Chapter 5) and the killing of a slave (Chapter 10) are read once, calmly and without extra detail; no sound effects, drawings or re-enactments.
Discuss idol worship as part of the story; do not mock people of other beliefs today. Abraham’s question “Don’t you understand?” is not a model for classroom language.

Keep to what each chapter says; do not add legends or details about the Ka’ba, Hajj or Zamzam that are not in the book. In Chapter 14, “ancestor” means a person in the same family who lived many generations earlier (“After many years …”).

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The story of Abraham (pbuh) links one family’s journey with questions for every community: How we check what we believe, how we welcome people who arrive from far away, how we value water, and how a place can be open to people of all colors.

themes.title: Look, ask and check:
themes.description: Abraham saw that the stone objects could not move or hear, and he asked “Could this be …?” before deciding (Chapters 1 and 3). Practise checking information before sharing it, at school and online.

themes.title: People on a journey:
themes.description: Abraham left Babylon and traveled a long, hot and tiring journey to other lands (Chapter 11). Talk about how it feels to arrive in a new place and how a class can welcome a new student.

themes.title: Water is a gift:
themes.description: Hagar found no water in the valley, and the Zamzam water later became “a gift from Allah in the middle of the desert” (Chapters 12–13). Connect this with saving water today.

themes.title: A place for all colors:
themes.description: Abraham “built a special place for Muslims of all colors” (Chapter 14). Discuss how our school can be a place where everyone feels welcome.

actions: Make a class poster with three ways to save water at school.
Write a short welcome card in English for a new student in your school.
Before you share a message online, ask one checking question: “Is this true? How do I know?”

exitTicket: One thing that happened in today’s chapter, and the sentence that shows it, is …
One language pattern I found today, with an example from the story, is …
One sentence about my own life with today’s pattern is …

miniProject.title: Abraham’s Journey Map
miniProject.desc: In groups, draw a simple map of the places in the book: Babylon, Syria and Palestine, the quiet valley near Safa and Marwah, and Mecca. At each place write one sentence from the book and one sentence of your own with a Language Focus pattern (for example “decided to …”, “Suddenly, …”, “still …”). Present the map to the class in two minutes.

reflectivePrompt.title: Trust and Effort
reflectivePrompt.desc: Hagar believed that Allah would protect them, and she also looked for food and water and ran from hill to hill. Write five or six sentences about a time you hoped for something and also worked hard for it. What did you do? What happened in the end?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value with a small action learners can do this week. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Learners separate what people believed from what the text shows, and they quote before they explain.

items.label: D10 Humility / D12 Patience
items.value: Accepting a mistake, staying calm and not giving up are treated as observable actions.

items.label: D16 Responsibility / D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Duties and help (“had to guide”, “I will help you for sure”) are connected with real tasks at home and school.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Belief and difference are discussed respectfully, without mocking people.

professionalDevelopment.intro: Use these steps to plan your own development with this book: rate yourself on the EPG areas with this book’s chapters, let a colleague observe one of two lessons, keep a short log after each chapter, run one small classroom enquiry, work with colleagues, and agree on scoring before the End-of-Level Test.

peerObservation.focus: Explain what the sun helped Abraham understand: Allah is the Creator and the sun is a creation.
lookFor: Instruction: In groups of four, each person gets one event card. Put your card in the right place on the board timeline and read your sentence from the story.
Check questions: How many cards does each person get? (one) / What do you read? (the sentence from the story)

While learners work: Check that the sunset card comes before the card about Abraham becoming a Messenger. In Activity 3, ask learners to explain each correction aloud. In Class duties, listen for no “will” in the If part.

peerObservation.focus: Say what Nimrod claimed and what question Abraham asked him.

While learners work: Read the slave part once yourself in a calm voice. Check that Nimrod’s claim and Abraham’s test are in different boxes. In the Can you challenge, keep claims harmless.

reflectionLog: After each chapter, answer the chapter’s “After the lesson” question in one or two sentences.

metadata.title: Prophet Abraham A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Look • Listen • Read • Check • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who study the story of Prophet Abraham at home or on their own.
learningGoals: Understand the 14 chapters of the story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh).
Find the answer sentence in the story.
Learn the Word Notes of each chapter.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in your own sentences.
Turn calm trust, humility and working together into small actions.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Answer the Quick Challenge before you read the feedback.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 14.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One person in the story I want to remember, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 14 chapters. Make a small plan before Chapter 1. A plan helps you keep going.
points: Choose your days. For example: two chapters a week.
If you like, choose a weekly goal in your Seyahatname. A new week starts on Monday.
Write one goal for this book: “At the end, I want to …”.
Save new words to My words. Review them after one day, after three days and after one week.
Before Chapter 1, open section 10, “Look Back”, and answer the “I can” questions.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter at a Time
sections.text: Study one chapter in one sitting. It takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” to see the steps for your chapter.
points: Look at the title and the picture.
Listen and follow the text.
Read one paragraph at a time.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Listen and Read
sections.text: Every chapter has audio. Listen first, then read.
points: First time: Listen for the main idea.
Second time: Follow the words with your eyes.
Stop the audio and say one short sentence again.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes and Hotspots
sections.text: Each chapter has underlined words. Tap a word to see its Word Note. Place names like Babylon and Mecca open a short note about the place. Tap the hotspots on the picture for short notes.
points: Read the word in its sentence first.
Guess the meaning, then check the Word Note.
Write the word and one sentence in your notebook.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Each chapter has one Quick Challenge. Answer first, then read the feedback.
points: Wrong answer? Find the answer sentence.
Read it again.
Try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has four Language Focus activities. Do them after you understand the chapter. They use sentences from the story.
points: Activity 1: look at a story sentence and its meaning.
Activities 2 and 3: practise the words and forms.
Last activity (Say It): Write or say three to five sentences of your own.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: It is fine to find a chapter hard. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Listen to one paragraph only.
Read two or three lines at a time.
Look at the picture and the hotspots again.
Learn only two words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Story
sections.text: The story of Prophet Abraham (pbuh) is about thinking, good manners, calm trust, humility and working together. Turn each value into one small action.
points: Thinking: Look and check before you believe (Chapters 1 and 3).
Good manners: Ask questions politely, even when you do not agree (Chapter 2).
Calm trust: Stay calm in a hard moment (Chapters 7 and 8).
Humility: Accept your mistake and do not be arrogant (Chapters 8 and 10).
Trust and hard work: Trust Allah and also do your best (Chapter 12).
Working together: Help your family with an important job (Chapter 14).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 14, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Master Glossary
Places & People
Vocabulary Challenge
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back: My Level and My Learning
sections.text: Answer these questions before Chapter 1 and again after the Final Challenge. For each one, say: not yet, a little or yes. They come from the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2020) for level A2. One book is one step, not a test.
points: Reading: “I can understand short narratives and descriptions of someone’s life composed in simple language.”
Speaking: “I can tell a story or describe something in a simple list of points.”
Writing: “I can produce a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like ‘and’, ‘but’ and ‘because’.”
Mediation: “I can convey the main point(s) involved in short, simple texts on everyday subjects of immediate interest, provided these are expressed clearly in simple language.”
What helped me most in this book?
What was hard, and what did I do about it?
What will I do in a different way in my next book?
